newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian utilities seen as takeover targets.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian utilities seen as takeover targets.

text.p: The small size of the Australian market would make Australian utilities in a de-regulated industry natural victims of takeovers, Michael Sargent, chief executive of Canberra-based ACTEW Corp Ltd, said on Wednesday.

Sargent, addressing the annual Electricity Supply Association of Australia Ltd conference, predicted that as Australian governments increasingly exited utility ownership, they would opt for the regulator's role.
That would put more utility ownership in private hands and result in more mergers between utilities, he said.

"Australian (utilities are) being positioned to be taken over because they do not understand that they are small in the world context," he said. "Almost universally in the developed world we are seeing a strong direction toward mergers and acquisitions as key strategies for growth," he said.

Factors behind a "frantic period of mergers and acquisitions" were low rates of return on investment, low growth rates, significant cash reserves and the need for size and diversity, he said. Mergers resulted from a need to grow as a means of survival in a competitive market, he said.

Australian regulators -- who made business life difficult with their "don't argue" approach -- were more likely to allow horizontal integration (expansion into other utility businesses) than vertical integration (expansion along the supply chain).

Horizontal integration involved complexity of regulatory and legislative frameworks, but had the advantage of creating competition between regulators, he said. Geographic diversification also did not attract opposition from regulators.

But vertical integration, which captured the value chain and economies of scale and scope, had the highest regulatory risk and was exposed to technology risk with potential for stranded assets, Sargent said.
Savings of 15 percent to 25 percent of total operating costs were readily achievable in horizontal integration of water and energy businesses, he said.
Sargent heads a corporatised utility which provides energy, water and wastewater management services in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT).
All its shares are presently held by the ACT government.
Answering questions, Sargent said ACTEW was considering investing in telecommunications, which provided a natural extension for utilities which understood networks.
The group had no pretentions to invest on a Rupert Murdoch scale and saw telecommunications as the wildcard in the utilities deck, he said.
Water supply would be the best-performing utility business in the next decade, he said.
